title: Sub-base-two exact maximum acyclic subgraph
formal: Do there exist constants \(1<c<2\), \(K\ge1\), an integer \(a\ge0\), and one uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every unweighted directed graph on \(n\) vertices, outputs a maximum-cardinality acyclic spanning subgraph in at most \(Kc^n(n+1)^a\) bit operations? The exponent parameter is the number of vertices, and the graph class and computational model are specified below.
why: Many ordering problems admit exact algorithms whose time grows like two to the number of vertices. Maximum acyclic subgraph is a basic test of whether directed precedence constraints permit a fixed exponential improvement, without restricting the input graph or accepting an approximate ordering.
status_note: The sub-base-two question is explicitly open in the 2013 seminar source. The checked July 2026 algorithm has a different parameter and does not settle it. Later searches through 2026-09-16 are bounded.

progress.text: The vertex-ordering paper records \(O^*(2^n)\) time with exponential space and \(O^*(4^n)\) time with polynomial space for directed feedback arc set.
Eunjung Kim’s seminar question asks whether maximum acyclic subgraph has an exact algorithm with a fixed exponential base below two.
The spanning-tree preprint studies above-guarantee parameterizations for integral and rational weights, with a parameter different from vertex count.

sentences: Maximum acyclic subgraph retains as many arcs of a directed graph as possible without retaining a directed cycle.
The source question asks for an exact algorithm whose running time has a fixed exponential base below two in the number of vertices.
The card specifies deterministic bit complexity, arbitrary unweighted directed graphs and an actual optimum arc set as output.
Known parameterized and approximation results do not automatically improve that worst-case vertex-count bound.
A resolution would clarify whether this basic precedence-ordering problem can beat the longstanding base-two exact-algorithm benchmark.

definitions:
An input consists of \(n\ge0\) and an \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. It represents \(D=([n],A)\), with one possible arc for each ordered pair of distinct vertices. Both opposite arcs between a pair may occur. There are no parallel copies, loops, weights, bounds on degree or density, connectivity promises, or restrictions to tournaments or planar graphs. The vertex number is encoded in binary along with the full matrix; the empty graph is allowed.

For \(B\subseteq A\), the spanning subgraph \(([n],B)\) is acyclic when it contains no directed cycle: there are no pairwise distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\) with \(k\ge2\) and arcs \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in B\) for every cyclic index \(i\). All original vertices remain, including isolated vertices. Define
\[
\operatorname{mas}(D)=\max\{|B|:B\subseteq A,\ ([n],B)\text{ is acyclic}\}.
\]
The output is the binary incidence vector of a subset \(B\subseteq A\) with \(|B|=\operatorname{mas}(D)\). Merely producing an inclusion-maximal acyclic set does not meet this task.

An algorithm is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program, with ordinary bit-cost input access, computation and output. Its worst-case running time, including all preprocessing, is bounded as stated on every valid graph. It has no oracle, random instructions or advice depending on \(n\), and there is no independent polynomial-space requirement. The constants \(c,K,a\) and the program are independent of the graph and its order. Polynomial factors in the input size can be written as polynomial factors in \(n+1\), since the matrix has \(n^2\) entries.

The required improvement is a fixed exponential base below two. Equivalently one can absorb the polynomial factor into a slightly larger base still below two and require a bound \(K'(c')^n\) with \(c'<2\). A factor saving that leaves exponential base two is insufficient. Exact output is part of this computational task, rather than an invitation to estimate a numerical benchmark value.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of such an algorithm, its exact optimal output and the worst-case bit-complexity bound for all valid inputs, or a complete Lean proof that no such constants and algorithm exist. Conditional lower bounds do not prove this unconditional negation. Algorithms for a proper graph subclass, approximation algorithms, or bounds exponential in the number of deleted arcs rather than vertices do not by themselves settle the assertion. No \(1/100\) additive tolerance applies to the asymptotic running-time target.

context_blocks.text: The inherited title did not specify the missing resource bound. Section 6.4 of the 2013 seminar report asks for an exact algorithm with exponential base strictly below two, parameterized by the number of vertices. This card makes the deterministic, unweighted adjacency-matrix branch explicit.

The 2012 vertex-ordering paper gives \(O^*(2^n)\) time and space for directed feedback arc set, where the star suppresses polynomial factors. Its complementary arc set is a maximum acyclic subgraph, so the exact optimization objectives have the same running-time baseline.

The retained arcs need only be consistent with some vertex ordering; deleting vertices is a different optimization problem. Similarly, the nearby arity-three ordering question in the seminar report is distinct from this card’s binary precedence constraints.

The 2026 spanning-tree paper gives algorithms parameterized by the amount \(k\) above a spanning-tree lower bound. Its dependence \(2^{k^{O(1)}}\) for integral weights does not provide a fixed base below two as a function of the vertex count on arbitrary inputs.
The requested bound allows exponential storage. Adding a polynomial-space condition or substituting a faster algorithm on a restricted degree class would change the target.
